text.title: Ops Metrics Basics Core Rules
text.summary: 10 testable rules every application of `Ops Metrics Basics` must enforce. Each rule pairs a binary check with a sourced rationale. Metric categories, the rule for choosing the right metrics, and an essential metrics table for solo operators.

section.title: Background
section.p: Five categories: North Star (ultimate success measure — active users or revenue), Leading (predict future outcomes — sign-ups, trial starts), Lagging (measure past results — revenue, churn), Input (actions you control — emails sent, ad spend), Output (results you want — conversions, revenue).

Minimum viable set with review frequency: Revenue (daily), MRR/ARR (weekly), active paying customers (weekly), churn rate (monthly), CAC (monthly), LTV (monthly), profit margin (monthly), runway (monthly). Do not add metrics beyond this set until the business has a dedicated operator for each new metric.

rule.statement: Set MUST contain 5-10 metrics. Fewer leaves blind spots; more dilutes ownership. Reject configs with > 10 board / weekly metrics.

rationale.source: Andy Grove HBR Output Management; OpenView 2023 SaaS benchmarks

rule.rationale: Cognitive limit on metric reasoning — beyond 10 metrics nobody can hold the system in their head, ownership decays, alerts get ignored.

rule.statement: Each metric MUST have one canonical SQL / formula stored alongside the config. Recomputations across tools forbidden — single source of truth.
rule.rationale: Same name + different formula across reports produces uncomparable numbers + heated meetings. Locked formula prevents drift.

rule.statement: Each metric MUST carry an explicit target value AND an alert threshold. Metrics without targets are observation, not management.
rule.rationale: Without target the metric is a thermometer not a thermostat. Alert threshold makes the metric actionable — change behaviour, not just report.

rule.statement: Cadence MUST be tiered: daily pulse (<= 3 metrics, automated), weekly review (5-10 metrics, owner-led), monthly deep-dive (segments, cohorts). Single weekly-only cadence is forbidden.

rationale.source: Tomasz Tunguz weekly business review; ProfitWell ops cadences

rule.rationale: Tiered cadence matches metric latency. Daily catches fires; weekly catches trends; monthly catches structural shifts. Single cadence misses two of three.

rule.statement: Each metric MUST name a single human owner. Group owners ('marketing', '#growth') are rejected — accountability decays without a name.
rule.rationale: Group-owned metrics rot. Named owner has lever to drive the metric + answer for misses at the review.

rule.statement: Track at most 10 metrics at any time; include exactly one north star metric, two to three leading indicators, and two to three lagging measures of financial health.
rule.rationale: Tracking too many metrics produces analysis paralysis and dilutes ownership. Fewer metrics with clear owners and targets produce faster decisions and clearer accountability.

rule.statement: Prefer actionable metrics (metrics you can change with a specific intervention) over vanity metrics (metrics that look good but don't inform decisions).
rule.rationale: Vanity metrics (total sign-ups all-time, page views) feel good to track but provide no decision signal. Actionable metrics (CAC by channel this month, churn rate) point to specific interventions.

rule.statement: Use the simplest stack that answers your questions: Stripe → Google Sheets → Looker Studio covers 80% of solopreneur needs before a data warehouse is justified.
rule.rationale: Complex analytics stacks require maintenance overhead that consumes time that could be spent on the business. Looker Studio's Stripe connector provides MRR, churn, and cohort data without custom SQL.

rule.statement: Set targets with three-level status thresholds: green (within 10% of target), yellow (10-20% below target), red (more than 20% below target); review red metrics in the next daily check-in.
rule.rationale: Binary pass/fail targets produce false urgency and panic. Three-level thresholds match response effort to deviation severity and prevent over-reaction to normal variance.

rule.statement: When preconditions in Applies If fail OR any item in Skip If triggers, do not run this methodology. Document the skip rationale in the artefact's parent log.
rule.rationale: Misapplied methodologies are worse than no methodology — they consume review cycles and produce false confidence.
